analogy.p: A single person pushing a car barely moves it, but a coil is like many people lining up and pushing in the same direction: each turn of wire adds its own small field, and inside the coil they all push along the same line so the fields add up to a big, uniform field. Adding an iron core is like bringing in extra helpers who join in as soon as the push starts. The analogy breaks down because the 'pushes' are fields that add as vectors, and outside the coil the fields partly cancel instead of adding.
analogy.t: A crowd of people all pushing the same way

bullets: State that a **current in a conductor produces a magnetic field** around the conductor.
Describe the **shape** of the field around a straight wire (concentric circles) and how its **strength** varies with current and distance.
Explain how **reversing the current reverses the field direction**.
Draw the field of a **solenoid** and state that it is **strong and uniform inside**.
Explain how a solenoid **increases the magnetic effect** of the current compared with a single wire.
Describe an **electromagnet** (solenoid with an iron core) and the factors that change its strength.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This spec point (AQA 4.7.2) is about the **magnetic field produced by an electric current**. You must know that a current-carrying wire has a magnetic field around it, how its **strength and direction** depend on the current, what happens when the wire is shaped into a **solenoid**, and how an **electromagnet** works. You should be able to **draw the field patterns** for a straight wire and a solenoid and explain why the solenoid arrangement increases the magnetic effect. It matters because electromagnets and the motor effect underpin motors, relays, loudspeakers and generators.

bullets: A **current-carrying conductor** is surrounded by a **magnetic field**.
The field exists **only while the current flows**: no current, no field.
A compass needle near the wire **deflects** when the current is switched on, showing the wire's field is stronger than the Earth's field locally.
The effect is larger with a **larger current** and nearer the wire.
The field is produced by **moving charges** (electrons in the wire), not by the metal being magnetic; a copper wire has a field even though copper is non-magnetic.
This is the reverse of the **generator effect**, where a moving magnetic field produces a current.
core.h: A current produces a magnetic field
core.p: Whenever **charge flows**, there is a magnetic field around it. A wire carrying an electric current therefore behaves like a magnet while the current flows, and the field disappears as soon as the current is **switched off**. You can show this by placing a **plotting compass** near a wire: when the current flows the needle turns, and when it is switched off the needle returns to pointing north. This link between electricity and magnetism is the basis of electromagnetism.

bullets: Field lines are **circles around the wire**, perpendicular to the wire.
Lines are **closer together near the wire**: the field is strongest at the wire and weakens with distance.
Increasing the **current** makes the field **stronger** (lines closer together in diagrams).
The field does not have poles in the way a bar magnet does.
With a compass: a ring of compasses around the wire all point tangent to the circle in the same rotational direction.
On diagrams the current is shown as a **dot (out of the page)** or a **cross (into the page)**.
core.p: Around a long straight wire the magnetic field lines are **concentric circles** in a plane at right angles to the wire, centred on the wire. The lines are closest together near the wire, where the field is **strongest**, and get further apart with distance, showing the field **weakens as you move away**. The direction of the lines depends on the direction of the current, and a compass placed around the wire will point along a circle.

bullets: Current **out of the page (dot)**: field lines go **anticlockwise**.
Current **into the page (cross)**: field lines go **clockwise**.
**Reverse the current = reverse the field direction**; the shape and strength stay the same.
Right-hand grip rule: **thumb = current direction**, **fingers = field direction**.
Conventional current flows from the **positive to the negative** terminal of the cell.
When asked 'what happens to the compass if the current is reversed', say it turns round and points the other way.
core.h: Direction of the field: reversing the current
core.p: The direction of the field depends on the direction of the **conventional current**. **Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field**, so a compass needle that turned one way now turns the opposite way. A handy rule is the **right-hand grip rule**: point your right thumb in the direction of the conventional current and your curled fingers show the direction of the field lines. (The grip rule itself is not named in the AQA spec but is a quick way to find direction.)

bullets: A solenoid is a **long coil of wire carrying a current**.
Inside the solenoid the field is **strong and uniform**: parallel, equally spaced lines in the middle.
Outside the field is **like that of a bar magnet**, with N and S ends.
Each loop produces a circular field; inside the coil all the loop fields point the **same way and add up** (superpose).
Between neighbouring turns, the fields **cancel**, leaving a smooth, nearly straight field inside.
More turns closer together means more loops adding their fields, so the field is stronger.
Therefore a solenoid with the **same current** gives a **stronger magnetic effect** than a single wire.
core.h: Why coiling a wire makes the field stronger: the solenoid
core.p: A **solenoid** is a long coil of wire. Bending the wire into a coil makes the magnetic effect of the current much greater, because the **field lines from each turn of wire add together** inside the coil, giving a **strong, uniform field** along the middle of the solenoid. Outside, the field is weaker and is shaped like the field of a **bar magnet**. Compared with a single straight wire, the same current produces a far stronger field because the field is **concentrated into a small space**.

bullets: Draw **straight, parallel, equally spaced lines** inside the solenoid, with arrows.
Draw **loops outside** that leave one end and return to the other end; arrows from N to S outside the magnet.
The end where field lines **emerge** is the **north pole**.
Reversing the current **swaps N and S ends**.
The pattern is the same as that of a **bar magnet**, which is why a solenoid is called an electromagnet when used with a core.
Check diagrams: lines must not cross and must be continuous through the coil.
core.h: Field pattern of a solenoid and its poles
core.p: The field lines of a solenoid run **through the inside from the south end to the north end**, then loop round **outside** from the north end back to the south end, just like a bar magnet. The **ends of the solenoid act as poles**. To find which end is north, use the grip rule for coils: curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of the current round the coils, and your **thumb points to the north pole**. Reversing the current reverses the poles.

bullets: Electromagnet = **solenoid + iron core**.
The core becomes an **induced magnet**, strengthening the field.
Soft iron is used because it **magnetises and demagnetises easily**; steel would stay magnetised.
The magnet works **only while current flows**: switching off removes the field.
The **poles reverse** if the current is reversed.
Compared with permanent magnets, electromagnets are **stronger, adjustable and controllable**.
core.p: An **electromagnet** is a **solenoid with a soft iron core**. The iron core is a magnetic material, so it becomes an **induced magnet** in the solenoid's field and adds its own magnetic field to the solenoid's, making the total field **much stronger**. Soft iron is chosen because it is easy to magnetise and **loses its magnetism quickly** when the current is switched off. This makes electromagnets useful because they can be **switched on and off**.

bullets: **Increase the current**: use more cells or a variable power supply with a higher potential difference.
**More turns of wire**: more loops each adding to the field.
**Add or enlarge the soft iron core**.
**Turns closer together** (coil more tightly) increases the field in the middle.
Investigation: independent variable (e.g. number of turns); dependent variable (number of paper clips lifted); control the current, core and wire.
Safety: a high current heats the wire, so use a variable resistor and don't leave the current on for long.
Link to calculations: more current means more energy dissipated as heat (P = I^2R), which is a limit on strength.
core.h: Factors affecting the strength of an electromagnet
core.p: The strength of an electromagnet can be increased in three main ways: increase the **current** through the coil, increase the **number of turns** of wire on the coil, or put in an **iron core** (or a larger core). Making turns closer together (a shorter solenoid with the same turns) also increases the field inside. A strong electromagnet can pick up more iron objects, so strength is often measured by counting paper clips or measuring the mass lifted.

bullets: **Scrap-yard crane:** the electromagnet picks up iron and steel when on and **releases it when switched off**.
**Relay:** a small current magnetises the core, attracts an iron armature and closes a second circuit.
**Electric bell:** the electromagnet attracts a striker; a break in the circuit makes it spring back, repeating.
**Circuit breaker:** too much current magnetises the core strongly enough to open the switch.
**Loudspeakers and motors:** use the interaction of an electromagnet's field with a permanent magnet's field (motors and loudspeakers point).
**Electric motors** use coils in a magnetic field to produce rotation (see the motors point).
core.p: Electromagnets are useful wherever a magnetic force needs to be **controlled** by a current. Because they can be switched on and off, they are used in scrap-yard cranes, electric bells, relays, circuit breakers and door locks. In a **relay** a small current in an electromagnet pulls a switch closed to turn on a larger current in a separate circuit. You may be asked to explain how a device works in terms of what happens when the current is switched on and off.

bullets: Dot = current **towards** you (out of paper); cross = current **away** from you (into paper).
Wire: draw at least **3 circles** with **increasing gaps** and **arrows**.
Solenoid: **straight lines inside**, loops outside, arrows N to S outside.
Label **N and S** using the right-hand grip rule.
If asked how to make the field in the solenoid stronger on the diagram, show lines **closer together**.
Never let field lines cross or end in empty space.
core.h: Drawing and interpreting current and field diagrams
core.p: Diagram questions need careful use of conventions: a **dot** shows the current coming out of the page, a **cross** shows it going into the page. Field lines must have arrows, be circles centred on the wire, and become further apart as they go outward. For a solenoid, draw the inside lines first (straight and parallel), then add the loops outside from N to S. Always label the poles if asked and show the direction of the current with an arrow.

bullets: **Motor effect:** current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force (quantified by F = BIl in the next spec point).
**Electric motors and loudspeakers** both use an electromagnet in a permanent magnet's field.
**Generator effect and transformers** rely on changing magnetic fields in coils on iron cores.
**Electricity:** current, potential difference and power determine heating and strength.
**Permanent vs induced magnets:** the iron core is an induced magnet.
**Circuit symbols:** be able to include cell, switch, ammeter and variable resistor in a circuit for an electromagnet.
core.p: The magnetic field of a current is the key to the **motor effect** (motors and loudspeakers point): a wire carrying a current in an external magnetic field feels a force because its own field interacts with the external one. The reverse process is the **generator effect**, where a changing magnetic field induces a potential difference. **Transformers** use two coils wound on an iron core. Electromagnet strength depends on current, linking to **Electricity (4.2)** and heating effects, and the induced magnetism of the core links back to permanent and induced magnets (4.7.1).

bullets: Explain **why** more current gives a stronger field: more charge moving per second, so each turn contributes more.
Explain **why** more turns give more field: more loops adding their fields in the same direction inside the coil.
Explain **why** an iron core strengthens the field: it becomes a strong induced magnet in the solenoid's field.
Explain **why** the field in the middle is uniform: contributions from all turns add up smoothly and the fields between turns cancel.
Use the term **'uniform'** only for parallel, equally spaced lines.
Link to energy: an electromagnet needs a continuous supply of energy (current) to maintain its field, unlike a permanent magnet.
core.p: There is no separate Higher-only content in this spec point, but top answers explain **why** each change increases the field. Increasing current means more charge flowing past each point each second, which produces a stronger field around each turn. More turns means more loops each contributing to the field in the same direction. An iron core multiplies the field because the core's domains line up with the solenoid's field and add their own field.

exam: **Command words:** 'draw' needs correct shape plus arrows; 'explain' needs a reason with 'because'; 'describe' needs a sequence or pattern.
**1-mark:** 'what is produced when a current flows in a wire?' - a magnetic field.
**Drawing the wire's field (2-3 marks):** concentric circles, increasing gaps outwards, arrows showing direction.
**Drawing a solenoid field (3 marks):** straight parallel lines inside, bar-magnet loops outside, arrows N to S.
**Ways to increase strength (3 marks):** increase current, add more turns, add an iron core.
**Explain why a solenoid is stronger (3-4 marks):** fields from each turn add together inside; concentrated; uniform.
**Electromagnet vs permanent magnet (2-3 marks):** can be switched on/off; strength can be varied; poles can be reversed.
**Investigation questions:** identify independent, dependent and control variables; count paper clips or measure mass lifted; repeat for reliability.
**6-mark plans:** give a method, the variables, safety (heating) and how you would present the results as a graph.
**Graph tips:** plot number of paper clips against number of turns or current; describe the trend (directly proportional if a straight line through origin).

mistakes.r: It is a set of concentric circles around the wire.
mistakes.w: The field of a straight wire is like a bar magnet's.

mistakes.r: Field lines are circles around the wire, perpendicular to it.
mistakes.w: Field lines are straight lines away from the wire.

mistakes.r: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field; the strength is the same.
mistakes.w: Reversing the current makes the field weaker.

mistakes.r: Any wire carrying a current produces a field because moving charges make fields.
mistakes.w: A copper wire has no magnetic field because copper isn't magnetic.

mistakes.r: It uses a soft iron core which loses magnetism when the current is off.
mistakes.w: An electromagnet uses a steel core.

mistakes.r: More turns increase the strength because each turn adds to the field.
mistakes.w: More turns means a weaker field because it is longer.

mistakes.r: It is the field inside that is strong and uniform; outside is like a bar magnet.
mistakes.w: The field outside the solenoid is uniform.

mistakes.r: Poles depend on current direction and swap if the current is reversed.

summary: You must know that a current in a conductor produces a magnetic field, describe and draw the circular field around a straight wire and the strong, uniform field inside a solenoid, explain why coiling a wire increases the magnetic effect, and describe how an electromagnet works and how its strength can be changed. It matters because electromagnets and the motor effect are used in many devices.

terms.d: The production of a magnetic field by an electric current.
Circular field lines around a current-carrying conductor, in a plane perpendicular to the wire.
The direction of flow of positive charge, from positive to negative terminal.
A long coil of wire that produces a magnetic field when a current flows.
A field with the same strength and direction everywhere; shown by parallel, equally spaced lines.
A solenoid with an iron core; a magnet that can be switched on and off.
A magnetic material that is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism quickly when the current is switched off.
A material that becomes a magnet when placed in a magnetic field.
One complete loop of wire in a coil.
Thumb along the conventional current, curled fingers show the field direction.
Small compass used to show the direction of a magnetic field at a point.
A switch operated by an electromagnet that allows a small current to control a larger one.
The piece of iron in a relay or bell that is pulled by the electromagnet.
How strong the magnetic force is at a point; greater when field lines are closer together.
The energy transferred per unit charge, which drives the current through the coil.

worked.ans: Increase the current (more cells or a higher potential difference); wind more turns of wire on the nail; use a larger or better soft iron core. Each makes the magnetic field stronger so more paper clips are lifted.
worked.q: A student makes an electromagnet by winding insulated wire round an iron nail and connecting it to a cell. Give three ways she could increase the number of paper clips it picks up. (3 marks)
steps: Think about the factors: current, number of turns, core.
State each as a change with a direction: increase current, more turns, bigger/better core.
Add the effect: stronger magnetic field so more clips.

worked.ans: Each turn of the wire makes its own magnetic field. Inside the solenoid the fields from all the turns point in the same direction and add together, so the field is concentrated into a small space and is strong and uniform. A straight wire's field spreads out in circles and is much weaker for the same current.
worked.q: Explain why a solenoid produces a stronger magnetic field than a straight wire carrying the same current. (4 marks)
steps: Each turn of wire produces a circular magnetic field.
Inside the coil these fields point in the same direction, so they add together.
The field is concentrated in a small space and is uniform inside.
Hence the same current gives a much stronger field.

worked.ans: The filings form concentric circles centred on the wire, getting further apart away from the wire. When the current is reversed, the compass needle points the opposite way along the circle because the field direction reverses.
worked.q: A current flows through a straight wire that passes vertically through a horizontal card. Describe the pattern of iron filings and what happens to a compass placed on the card when the current is reversed. (3 marks)
steps: Filings form concentric circles around the wire.
Circles further apart as distance from wire increases (field weaker).
Reversing the current reverses the field direction so the compass needle turns through 180 degrees.
